places.name: The welcoming party
places.description: People are almost never arrived-at alone. A group is already assembled and already knows you are coming; experiencers say they were expected. The corpus's own name for it is the 'welcoming committee' or 'welcome party'. It ranges from a triangle of three to eighty figures at a distance to 'thousands and thousands'. The dominant emotion reported is not awe but recognition and hilarity — they are delighted, joyous, glad to see you.

aliases.note: the single most common self-coined phrase in the corpus for this

places.regex: (welcoming|welcome|greeting) (party|committee)|(greeted|welcomed) (me|us)[^.]{0,80}(heaven|the light|arrived|home|family|relatives|loved ones|other side|there)|(they|people|family|relatives|everyone|loved ones|souls|beings|angels) (were|was)[^.]{0,25}waiting for me|(there|were there) to (greet|welcome) me
sensory: a triangle or wedge formation with the closest relative at the point
the crowd extending back into shadow — 'shadows in the back' you still recognise
arms out, hands extended, embracing
joy and laughter rather than solemnity
no surprise on their side: 'I didn't show up and surprise anyone'

quotes.text: I did see many, many, many people there waiting for me, and they were all very joyous and very happy to see me. It was a huge welcoming party.
My welcoming committee, I called them. And at the very point of the triangle was my beautiful Grandad Sam
About 80 people were behind her a short distance off, and I could not see them clearly, but I knew they were there to welcome me.
it just felt like I was home, I was there, and they were my welcome party. And there were thousands and thousands of, I'm going to say beings

places.notes: Slightly MORE common among strongly-evidenced accounts (3.71% all vs 5.11% cv>=18), though the cv>=23 stratum is small (n=181) and drops back to 3.87%. An earlier draft of this regex included 'on the other side' and precision collapsed to ~50% because that phrase is a generic idiom for the afterlife in interview chatter; it was removed. Note the negative case is also reported: Howard Storm's welcoming committee turns out to be deceptive and leads toward hell — the welcome is not always benign.

places.name: The dead of your own family
places.description: The people met are overwhelmingly your own dead: mother, father, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, cousins, spouses. They are recognised instantly, often before being seen clearly — recognition is by 'energy' or by knowing rather than by face. They typically do not explain themselves; they reassure, they say it is not your time, and several accounts note they are noticeably busy and involved, not idle.

aliases.term: family members on the other side

aliases.note: sometimes used interchangeably, sometimes distinguished from blood family

places.regex: (deceased|dead|departed|passed|late) (relatives|loved ones|family|friends|grandmother|grandfather|mother|father|brother|sister)|(relatives|loved ones|family members|ancestors) (who|that) (had )?(died|passed)|(saw|met|there (was|were)|greeted by) (my|his|her) (mother|father|dad|mom|brother|sister|uncle|aunt|cousin|son|daughter|husband|wife)[^.]{0,60}(who (had )?(died|passed)|had (died|passed)|was dead|standing|waiting|there)
sensory: recognised by energy or knowing rather than by sight
no aging or illness carried over
period clothing from the era each of them lived in
they hug, take your hand, put a hand out
communication is soundless (see telepathic-speech)

quotes.text: I was greeted by people I had known in the past. Um, relatives, my, uh, a grandpa was there, um, an aunt that had died just previous to this.
I saw thousands of people there, including my mom, grandmothers, and aunt, and an uncle. Everyone looked 25 to 30 years old.
there was no speech, it was all telepathic, I recognized instantly as my ICU patient

places.notes: This is the strongest evidential gradient in my whole region: 8.73% of all accounts, 19.89% of the best-evidenced (cv>=23) — a 2.3x enrichment, monotone across all four strata. The corpus's own structured coding agrees independently (deceased_relatives present in 39.9% all vs 58.6% cv>=23). Whatever produces high veridical-perception scores also produces encounters with the family dead. My regex is far more conservative than the structured coder's, so treat 8.73% as a floor, not a prevalence.

places.name: The grandparent at the front
places.description: Grandmothers and grandfathers are the single most frequently named individual greeters in the corpus — more often named than parents. They are usually described as standing at the front of the group, or as the first face resolved out of the light. The grandmother in particular is often the one who does the talking and the reassuring; several experiencers met a grandmother or great-grandmother they had never met in life and later identified her from family photographs.

aliases.note: used when the being is unidentified but feels like a grandmother

places.regex: (my (grandmother|grandma|grandmom|granny|nana|grandfather|grandpa|granddad|grandad|grandparents|great-grandmother|great-grandma))[^.]{0,90}(was|were) (there|waiting|standing|coming)|(saw|met|greeted by|there (was|were)) (my |his |her )?(grandmother|grandma|granny|nana|grandfather|grandpa|granddad|grandparents)
places.negative_regex: (grandmother|grandma|grandpa|granddad)[^.]{0,40}(raised me|babysat|farm|kitchen|house when I was|took me to (church|school))
sensory: restored to their thirties or fifties, not the age at which they died
'he looked so well' / 'she was youthful'
very large hands remembered from childhood
hair 'of fire' in one account; an angelic rather than elderly appearance
recognised from photographs only afterwards

quotes.text: And my grandfather was there. And he looked great. He had died at 71, but he looked about 35 or 40.
My grandma was waiting for me, my guardian angel was waiting for me.
they all looked younger than I even remembered them being, and you know, healthy and vibrant

places.notes: Nearly doubles in the well-evidenced strata (4.50% -> 8.70% at cv>=18). The bare noun 'grandmother' occurs in 36.66% of all transcripts, almost all of it biography — that is why this regex demands a meeting/waiting verb. Residual false positives are mostly childhood-memory sentences that happen to contain 'was there'.

places.name: Meeting someone you did not know had died
places.description: The veridical signature of this whole region: the experiencer meets a specific person on the other side, comes back, and only then learns that the person had died — sometimes hours or days earlier, sometimes decades. Experiencers who tell this rarely dwell on it; they report it flatly as the thing that convinced them. Several report the converse formula from the other direction: a being says 'what are you doing here, you're not dead'.

aliases.term: I didn't know she had died
I had no idea he had passed
the child no one had told me about
no one ever meets someone who isn't dead
aliases.note: the researcher's formulation, quoted back by experiencers

places.regex: (saw|met|there was|recognized|encountered)[^.]{0,70}(who|whom|that) I (didn'?t|did not) know (had )?(had )?(died|passed|was dead)|(didn'?t know|did not know|had no idea|wasn'?t aware|never knew|nobody (had )?told me|no one (had )?told me|didn'?t even know)( that)? (he|she|they|my [a-z-]+)[^.]{0,45}(had )?(just )?(died|passed|passed away|was dead|were dead)|(people|someone|somebody|a (person|man|woman|boy|girl))[^.]{0,50}(I|they) (didn'?t|did not) know (had )?(died|passed|was dead)
places.negative_regex: (didn'?t know|did not know|had no idea)( that)? (I|i) (was dead|had died)
sensory: the person appears at the age they would recognisably be, or younger
often a sibling who died before the experiencer was born
sometimes a name is given that the family later confirms
the recognition arrives before the reasoning does

quotes.text: I didn't know she had died, but I knew that was her there.
Well, I have met people in the Hereafter. I didn't know had died, among them young people.
My sister had a stillborn baby boy. What I didn't know is that they named him Steven.

places.notes: Genuinely rare and I am reporting the precision honestly as poor: roughly half the matches are after-death-communication dreams or waking visitations rather than during-NDE meetings, and a few are interviewers describing the phenomenon in the abstract. Doubles at cv>=13 (0.57% -> 1.15%), which is the direction you would expect if it is real, but n=35 total means these percentages are fragile. I deliberately excluded the far more common self-referential 'I didn't know I was dead' (which alone matches ~3.2% of the corpus) because that is a different phenomenon.

places.name: The children who were never born
places.description: A small but very consistent cluster: experiencers meet a miscarried, stillborn or aborted child, or a sibling who died as a baby before they were born. The child is not an infant — it is described as a fully developed soul, often aged forward to the years elapsed since the loss, and it initiates the contact ('hi, Mommy'). Separately, many accounts describe children simply playing in the landscape, not as anyone's dead in particular.

aliases.term: the child I never knew on Earth
a little boy / a little girl

places.regex: (my|the) (baby|babies|child|children|son|daughter|sister|brother|twin)[^.]{0,90}(miscar\w+|stillborn|abort\w+|never born|died as a (baby|child|infant)|i never (met|knew))|(met|saw|there was) (my|the|a) (baby|little (boy|girl)|child)[^.]{0,60}(i (had )?(lost|miscarried)|(who|that) (i|we) (lost|miscarried|never))
sensory: aged forward to match the years since the loss
carried by another dead relative and handed over
named — and the name matches one the family chose but never spoke aloud
children playing at what looks like school recess, with animals among them

quotes.text: I saw my sister who died as a baby. Now she was walking down to me and carrying my son.
the little girl says, yes, yes, you are. Uh, you know, I'm, I'm the child you aborted.

places.notes: Rare but rises monotonically with evidential strength (0.42% -> 1.10%). Some matches are the experiencer's own obstetric history rather than a meeting; I kept the regex tight rather than inflate the count. The broader pattern 'children playing / babies in heaven' matches 226 docs (3.66%) but with much lower specificity, so I did not use it as the measured figure.

places.name: Pets and animals
places.description: Dogs above all, then cats and horses. The pet is usually simply present rather than central — 'they were just there in support' — and several experiencers note the animal does not have its earthly body: one describes his childhood dog as a floating sphere of awareness that he merged with. Animals are also reported en masse in the landscape, unafraid and mixed in with children.

aliases.note: one experiencer's description of his dog's form

places.regex: (my|our|the|his|her) (dog|dogs|cat|cats|pet|pets|horse|horses|puppy|kitten)[^.]{0,60}(was|were) (there|waiting|with me|running|greeted)|(pets|animals|dogs|our animals)[^.]{0,40}(in heaven|on the other side|were there|waiting for)|(saw|met) my (dog|cat|pet|horse)
sensory: no fur or legs — awareness without an animal body
recognised instantly anyway, by name
greeting is wordless and mutual absorption rather than licking or jumping
animals unafraid, mixed with children, in the landscape

quotes.text: I was nine years old, and my dog Skippy was there. My dog was there.
Especially my dog was there in the afterlife. They have souls.
Some of my pets were there. I didn't talk to any of them. I didn't need to.

places.notes: Essentially flat across strata — no evidential enrichment, unlike the human dead. Precision is limited because 'my dog was there' also occurs in ordinary accident narratives (a dog present at the scene, a rescue dog). The corpus's own entity census records only 191 'animal' and 11 'deceased_pet' encounters across 11,885 entity records, consistent with genuine rarity.

places.name: Angels
places.description: The most-named non-human category in the corpus after God and Jesus. Wings are the contested detail: roughly as many experiencers say the angels had no wings as say they did, and several explicitly correct the expectation ('they didn't have wings — they were dressed in ornate gowns', 'they really were these orbs of light'). Where wings are reported they are large, soft, feather-bed-like, and used to enfold rather than to fly. Angels are frequently taller and more luminous than the human dead, and are described as escorts and protectors rather than as conversationalists.

aliases.note: some experiencers use this instead of 'angel' for the same figures

places.regex: (angels?|archangel\w*|angelic (being|figure|presence)s?)[^.]{0,60}(appeared|came|were there|was there|around me|beside me|greeted|took me|wings|carried|standing|surrounded)|(two|three|four|many|thousands of|several) angels|(saw|met|there (was|were)) (an? )?angel
places.negative_regex: (you'?re an angel|she was an angel|like an angel|angel investor|Angel(s)? (baseball|stadium))
sensory: taller and more illuminated than the human dead
wings 'like big soft beds', 'like a down comforter'
light blue sashes over white robes
no wings at all in many accounts — ornate gowns, or pure orbs of colour
touch feels like a light socket, but pleasant
singing described as 'mighty streams of living water'

quotes.text: these two angels, um, they didn't have wings. They were dressed in these ornate, beautiful dresses or gowns.
So I know we depict angels in very much this human form with these wings, but they really were these orbs of light.
They had brown robes on and they had golden belts around their waist, and they introduced themselves as my ministering angels

places.notes: Only mildly enriched in better-evidenced accounts (15.04% -> 17.13%), far less than the deceased relatives. False positives come from post-NDE angel beliefs and from the idiomatic 'you're an angel'. The corpus entity census logs 1,068 angel encounters plus 191 'angel' and 83 'guardian angel' raw identities, so this is a genuinely large category, not an artefact.

places.name: Guides, guardians and the one who comes to fetch you
places.description: A being whose role is transit and instruction rather than reunion. It introduces itself ('I'm Allan, I'm your spirit guide'; 'my name is Elizabeth, I am your guardian angel and I'm here to help you'), takes the experiencer by the hand, and leads them into the light, along a path, up a staircase or into a building. Guides are far more often described as functionally helpful than as adored. Many experiencers report the same guide continuing to speak to them for decades afterwards.

aliases.note: one experiencer's word for seven robed overseers

aliases.term: the gentleman there to greet me

places.regex: (spirit guides?|guardian angels?|my guides?( |,|\.)|the guide|a guide|spiritual guide|my (teacher|escort|helper))|(took (my|me by the) hand|held my hand|by the hand|took hold of my hand)[^.]{0,80}(led|walked|took|guided|brought|and we)|(escort\w*|accompan\w+|led me|guided me|took me) (to|through|into|up|along)[^.]{0,50}(light|tunnel|garden|city|realm|place|heaven|gate)
sensory: gives a personal name, which the experiencer usually cannot later trace
takes the hand — after which the unstable ground becomes walkable
vaguely human shape, sometimes deliberately made human-ish 'to make it easier for me to relate'
walks slightly ahead or slightly behind, never in front of the light
sometimes multiple: 'three original light beings that greeted me'

quotes.text: my name is Elizabeth. I am your guardian angel and I'm here to help you.
there's a jump from being in this room with this group of people to being in a much smaller room with only my guide.
And she takes me to a park bench where I see these two elderly people.

places.notes: The broadest place in my region and the one whose precision I trust least. Roughly 40% of matches are post-NDE ongoing guide relationships, general belief statements about guides, or interviewers using the term — not a guide encountered during the experience. The 'took my hand and led me' and 'led me to the light' sub-patterns are far cleaner (1.17% and 4.63% respectively, ~90% precision) and could be split out downstream if a tighter measure is wanted.

places.name: The council of elders
places.description: A seated, deliberative body — usually a semicircle or a long table, usually numbered (twelve, eleven, thirteen, three) — that reviews the life, lays out lessons, and rules on whether the experiencer returns. It is distinguished from the welcoming party by furniture and by procedure: there are tables, podiums, a chair in the centre, an order of speaking. Experiencers report humour rather than severity: the council chuckles, and knows what you are thinking before you say it.

aliases.term: a council of high spiritual beings

places.regex: (council of (elders|light|(the )?(twelve|12|11|nine|9|men))|council of (high )?(spiritual )?beings|(the|a) council[^.]{0,30}(elders|beings|souls|wise|met|sitting|table)|(12|twelve|thirteen|13) elders|elders (were|sat|sitting|around)|(a|the) (group|panel|circle) of elders)
places.negative_regex: (Council of (Nicaea|NAA|Trent|Biomedicine)|student council|city council|whole council of God|tribal elders|church elders|native elders)
sensory: a semicircular or very long table; podiums; benches on four sides
the experiencer seated or standing in the centre facing them
a fixed number, most often twelve
they laugh — and the laughter reveals that they have heard your thoughts
one account: seven robed 'monitors' with light pouring from their palms

quotes.text: There were 12 elders sitting at the table beside him.
What I have also experienced was the presence of a council of elders.
And I met the Council of 12.

places.notes: Flat across strata. The bare word 'council' matches 341 docs (5.5%) but most of that is the Council of Nicaea, student council, or tribal/church elders, which is why the negative_regex is long. Almost entirely absent from Christian-framed accounts and concentrated in secular/New Age framings — a clear case of cultural patterning of the same slot in the narrative (Christians describe standing before Jesus at the same journey position).

places.name: Robed figures
places.description: Beings identified chiefly by their clothing: white robes, brown robes with golden belts, tunics of loose-weave sack material, robes of many colours, dark hooded robes. Some are named (angels, Jesus), many are not — 'a strange robe figure who led me down a path'. The robe is often the only detail given, and several experiencers say the faces were deliberately indistinct or grey: 'our faces don't matter, it's our presence'.
places.regex: (robe|robes|robed)[^.]{0,50}(being|beings|figure|figures|man|men|woman|women|people|angel|angels|monk)|(being|beings|figure|figures|man|men|woman|women|people|angel|angels)[^.]{0,50}(in|wearing|wore|dressed in) (a |the |white |long |flowing )*(robe|robes|tunic|gown)|(hooded|cowl)
sensory: white, but also brown with golden belts, and 'robes of many colours'
light blue sashes
dark robes with dark hoods — smiling, giggling, bouncing (not menacing)
faces grey or featureless, neither male nor female
the robes are said to be worn because they are the most comfortable, not required

quotes.text: They had brown robes on and they had golden belts around their waist, and they introduced themselves as my ministering angels
I was greeted by a strange robe figure who led me down a path to the field.
They were in white robes, their faces kind of looked like gray, like they weren't male or female
They had dark robes and dark hoods, and they were right in front of me. And they were smiling and giggling

places.notes: Rises steadily with evidential strength (4.19% -> 7.18%). Note the corpus contradicts the stock iconography twice over: hooded figures are cheerful rather than sinister, and at least one experiencer complains that dramatised reconstructions with robes and 'little tiny wings' are cheesy.

places.name: Beings of light without form
places.description: Beings that have no body at all — orbs, spheres, balls of light, energy fields, 'light fragments', figures shining in different colours. Experiencers stress that they had no faces and yet were unmistakably individual and unmistakably known. Some accounts say the experiencer was one of these too: 'we're beings of light, really, is what we are'. This category shades into and often merges with angels, guides and the crowd of souls; the corpus does not police the boundary.

aliases.term: figures that were shining in all different colors

places.regex: (beings? of (light|pure light)|light beings?|luminous beings?|orbs? of light|balls? of light|(beings|figures) (made )?of (pure )?(light|energy))
sensory: no faces, but the outline of a body
colours 'more vibrant than you can imagine' — blues, yellows, purples
moving at speed through a matrix of connected lights
each one unique yet with no separation between them
they beam love at you as a felt force, not a message

quotes.text: they didn't have faces, they were just light, but they had almost like the shape of a body
And the three original light beings that greeted me were with me.
they're glowing golden lights that that I knew them, but I didn't know them in this lifetime.

places.notes: Flat to very slightly declining across strata. Overlaps heavily with whatever the singular 'being of light' place captures elsewhere in the map — my interest here is the PLURAL, formless, non-divine population, which is what the plural aliases pick up. The main false-positive source is post-NDE philosophising ('we're all beings of light trapped inside these meat sacks').

places.name: The crowd
places.description: Beyond the named greeters there is very often a mass — dozens, hundreds, thousands, 'a huge group of people, dozens and dozens and dozens', a kingdom 'populated by tremendous numbers of people'. The crowd is busy: working, learning, involved with the living. Experiencers report loving all of them and knowing all of them individually, which is one of the most reliably strange claims in the corpus.

aliases.term: the whole crowd extended far into the distance

places.regex: (group|crowd|thousands|hundreds|multitude|host|sea|army|circle) of (beings|souls|angels|spirits|entities|light beings)|(a|the) (group|crowd|circle) of (people|figures|beings)[^.]{0,70}(light|white|robe|waiting|greet|welcom|around me|surround|energ)
places.negative_regex: (group of people (at|in) (church|the office|work|school)|thousands of people (died|were killed|watched))
sensory: extends back into shadow — you know who each shadow is anyway
people from visibly different time periods, in period dress
no one old, no one sick, no one crying
they are working and learning, not idle
in some accounts they are past lives of the experiencer, not other people

quotes.text: there was a huge group of people, dozens and dozens and dozens, maybe even hundreds.
And I could see that there were many people, as populated by tremendous numbers of people. And I knew each and every one of them intimately.

places.notes: Nearly doubles from all accounts to the best-evidenced (3.74% -> 7.18%). An earlier unconstrained version ('group of people') matched 924 docs at ~30% precision — almost all ordinary biography — so the context clause is load-bearing. 'Soul family / soul group' alone matches 283 docs (4.58%) but is a New Age framing that runs the OTHER way across strata (5.26% all vs 2.76% cv>=23), so I kept it out of the measured regex and listed it only as an alias.

places.name: The presence you cannot see
places.description: Someone is there, usually behind or beside the experiencer, never looked at directly and often never seen at all — yet its identity is felt with certainty and its emotional quality (gentle, non-judging, patient) is the strongest thing about it. The corpus's own entity coder records 'presence_only' as a communication method 2,149 times. Several experiencers say they deliberately did not turn around.

aliases.term: somebody was standing next to me
an energy field with a presence

places.regex: (a|this|the|his|her|some) presence[^.]{0,70}(beside|next to|behind|with me|there|felt|sensed|loving|comforting)|(felt|sensed) (a|the|this|some) presence|presence (of (someone|somebody|a being)|behind me|next to me|beside me)|(someone|somebody|a being) (was )?(standing )?(behind|next to|beside) me[^.]{0,50}(couldn'?t see|never saw|didn'?t see|but I knew)
places.negative_regex: (in the presence of (the )?(press|media|company|management)|presence of mind|online presence|stage presence)
sensory: always slightly behind, or just at the shoulder
light emanating from behind you so the scene ahead looks black and white by comparison
no face is ever resolved
non-judging is the adjective used most often
communicates by prompting, not by asking

quotes.text: Somebody was standing next to me. I never saw them, I couldn't see them, but I felt that they were standing there
there was the presence next to me of what I felt was God.
it was an immediate feeling of, um, there is somebody

places.notes: Rises with evidential strength (12.18% -> 15.47%). Roughly 30% of matches are the devotional idiom 'the presence of God' used outside the experience, or post-NDE sensing of presences; I left them in rather than over-tune, since the phrase is genuinely continuous between the two uses in these narratives.

places.name: How the dead appear: restored
places.description: Uniformly, the dead are not as they died. Amputations, cancer, dementia, wheelchairs and old age are gone. The most commonly cited apparent age is the mid-twenties to mid-thirties regardless of the age at death, and several experiencers were unable to recognise a parent for that reason until afterwards. A recurring refinement: the being first appears at the age you would recognise, then visibly changes to its restored age once recognition has happened.

aliases.term: in the prime of their life

places.regex: (young again|in (his|her|their) prime|prime of (his|her|their) life|no longer (sick|ill|in pain|had cancer|in a wheelchair)|(looked|appeared|seemed) (so |really |very )?(healthy|young|whole|perfect|radiant|vibrant)|(looked|appeared) (to be )?(about |around )?(in (his|her|their) (20s|30s|twenties|thirties)|25|30|35)( years old)?|(he|she|they) (was|were) (whole|healed|restored|perfect) again|everyone looked young|no ?one (was|looked) (sick|old))
places.negative_regex: (when I was young|younger than I (was|am)|my younger (sister|brother)|looked young for (his|her) age)
sensory: mid-twenties to mid-thirties is the modal apparent age
eyes 'more light than eyes'
no wrinkles, no weight, no heaviness, no pain
period-appropriate clothing but a restored body inside it
the being may deliberately appear old first so you can identify them, then shift younger

quotes.text: the reason I didn't recognize him was because he was younger. He looked like my husband's age. He looked about 30 years old.
He appeared as an old man so he could be easily recognized, then changed to look younger, about thirty.
I saw thousands of people there, including my mom, grandmothers, and aunt, and an uncle. Everyone looked 25 to 30 years old.

places.notes: Clearly enriched in better-evidenced accounts (3.79% -> 5.66%). This regex is the third draft; the first two were swamped by 'when I was younger', which is why that phrase is in the negative_regex. Residual false positives are mostly the experiencer describing their OWN restored body rather than a greeter's, which is arguably the same phenomenon.

places.name: Strangers you already know
places.description: A distinct and very consistently worded experience: the experiencer meets beings they have certainly never met in this life, and knows them anyway — 'I knew them, but I didn't know where I knew them from'. The knowing is described as older than the lifetime ('we had known each other for eons'), and the inability to place them is reported as mildly frustrating rather than frightening. This is the strongest formal argument the corpus itself makes against the 'expectation fulfilment' explanation.

aliases.term: I knew them but I didn't know them
I felt like I knew her, though we'd never met
I knew each and every one of them intimately
I didn't know them in this lifetime

places.regex: ((knew|recognized) (them|him|her|everyone|every one|each)[^.]{0,80}(never met|didn'?t know|hadn'?t met|not in this life|from before|soul level|eons|always known|couldn'?t place)|knew (them|him|her) but (I )?didn'?t know|(felt|felt like) I knew (them|him|her)[^.]{0,40}(but|though|even though)|knew (each|every one) of them)
sensory: recognition arrives before any face is seen
people dressed from many different eras all recognised equally
no names attached to the recognition
the feeling is of resumed acquaintance, not introduction

quotes.text: they knew me and I knew that I knew them, but I just didn't know where I knew them from.
they're glowing golden lights that that I knew them, but I didn't know them in this lifetime.

places.notes: Rare but the wording is remarkably stereotyped, which is why precision is high despite the small n. Doubles at cv>=18 (0.65% -> 1.38%). Note two of the 40 matching documents are near-duplicate uploads of the same narrator (Sharon Milliman), so the true independent count is slightly lower.

places.name: Speaking without speaking
places.description: How the inhabitants communicate. Experiencers are near-unanimous that no mouths moved and no sound travelled, yet the exchange was complete and instant. Many stress it is faster and more complete than words — whole understandings arrive at once, and questions are answered before they are finished. Several bilingual experiencers note that language ceased to be a barrier. A minority report an additional audible voice that 'went through my bones' alongside the silent exchange.
places.regex: (telepath\w+|mind to mind|thought to thought|mind-to-mind|soul to soul|communicat\w+ (with|by|through) (thought|thoughts|our minds)|(spoke|speak|spoken|talked|communicated) without (words|speaking|(his|her|their|our|my) (mouth|lips))|no words were (spoken|needed|necessary)|didn'?t (use|need) (any )?words|without (moving|opening) (his|her|their|my) (mouth|lips))
sensory: no mouths move; some beings have no mouths at all
the answer arrives simultaneously with the question
thoughts are transparent in both directions — they laugh at what you have not said
one account describes it as communication in mathematics and music
an audible voice, when it occurs, is felt in the bones rather than the ears

quotes.text: I remember having a quick thought about we just talked without talking
she telepathically said to me to calm myself down she did not speak but I was listening to her
there was no speech, it was all telepathic, I recognized instantly as my ICU patient

places.notes: Monotone increase across every stratum (26.88% -> 34.81%), matching the corpus's own structured coding (telepathy 60.0% all vs 70.2% cv>=23) at a stricter threshold. Interesting tension: the corpus entity census records 'verbal' (3,900) MORE often than 'telepathy' (2,942) as the communication method, so silent exchange is dominant but not universal — a substantial minority of experiencers insist they heard an actual voice.

places.name: It is not your time
places.description: The near-formulaic sentence that ends the visit. It is delivered by a relative, a guide, an unseen voice or a religious figure, and is almost always some variant of 'it's not your time' or 'you have to go back'. Frequently it is repeated two or three times against the experiencer's protest. Reasons given are usually a task, a child, or unfinished purpose — rarely anything doctrinal.

aliases.note: the single most reproduced sentence in the whole corpus

aliases.term: it's not time to go yet
I do not wish to have you home yet

places.regex: (it'?s not your time|it was not (my|your) time|not yet your time|it wasn'?t (my|your|his|her) time|you have to go back|you must go back|you need to go back|you'?re going back|(told|said)[^.]{0,25}(I|you) (had|have) to go back|(sent|send) me back|being sent back|not your time (to (die|go|be here))?)
sensory: repeated, often three times, against protest
delivered without explanation or with a single reason: a child, a task, a message
sometimes pointed rather than spoken — a hand indicating the way out
sometimes a hand held up 'like a stop sign'
the experiencer usually argues, and loses

quotes.text: And then I hear this voice saying, "You have to go back. It's not your time."
I turned around, and I saw that it was my stepdad, and he says to me, he says, it's not your time.

places.notes: Mildly enriched in better-evidenced accounts and then flat. The corpus's own journey coding puts 'forced_return' at mean relative position 0.893 and 'choice_to_return' at 0.867, so this sits right at the hinge of the narrative. A small but striking counter-case exists: at least one experiencer (Venia Hill) was told the opposite — 'it WAS my time' — and returned anyway.

places.name: Not wanting to come back
places.description: The most emotionally loaded thing in this region and, in raw prevalence, one of the largest. Experiencers say plainly that they did not want to return, that they begged and pleaded to stay, that they grabbed hold of the being's legs, that they screamed no. The reason given is almost never fear of pain — it is that the place felt like home in a way earth never had. Many are still visibly upset about it decades later during the interview.

aliases.term: I didn't want to come back
I didn't want to go back
I pleaded with them to let me stay
wild horses couldn't drag me there

places.regex: (didn'?t want to (go|come) back|did not want to (go|come) back|didn'?t want to return|did not want to return|didn'?t want to leave|not want to go back|never want\w* to (go|come) back|wanted to stay (there|here|so)|(begg\w+|plead\w+)[^.]{0,55}(let me stay|to stay|don'?t (make|send) me|not to (go|send)|to let me))
places.negative_regex: (didn'?t want to (go|come) back to (work|school|prison|that job|my ex))
sensory: the word used over and over is 'home' — not heaven, home
grabbing, clinging, holding onto legs
screaming 'no' while being pushed backwards
still weeping about it in the interview, decades later
a minority report the opposite: an easy, almost comic acceptance ('yeah, I know, I've got to go back')

quotes.text: I didn't want to go back to my body. I wanted to go higher. I wanted to go to the next level.
I grabbed hold of his legs, and I grabbed hold of him tight, and I was begging him, "Please don't send me back. I don't want to go back."
There's a sense of being home like you will never have here. It was total home. And I didn't want to leave.
I remember this force pushing me backwards and I remember screaming no.

places.notes: Consistently ~25% more common in the well-evidenced strata. The explicit begging/pleading sub-pattern alone matches 98 docs (1.59% all, 3.31% cv>=23) — doubling in the best-evidenced accounts, the sharpest gradient of any sub-pattern I measured. Note the reciprocal grief: several accounts describe the being apologising, promising to meet again, or sending someone back WITH them.

places.name: The snap back
places.description: Re-entry is overwhelmingly violent and instantaneous, not gradual. The verbs are consistent across hundreds of accounts: slammed, snapped, sucked, shot, yanked, thrown, catapulted, whooshed, shoved, kicked. Several describe being drawn back down the tunnel the way they came; one describes it as 'the opposite of a cork getting pulled out of a bottle of wine'. Entry is usually through the top of the head, occasionally feet-first. Gentle descents exist but are rare (33 docs, 0.53%).
places.regex: (snapped|slammed|sucked|shot|yanked|jerked|thrown|thrust|catapult\w*|whooshed|zoomed|slam|snap|plopped|shoved|pushed|hurled|rammed|kicked|dropped|plunged|whoosh) (right )?back (down )?(in ?to|into|in) (my|the) (physical )?body|(sucked|pulled|yanked|snapped) back (down )?(through|into) the (tunnel|light)|like a (rubber ?band|bungee|slingshot)
sensory: entry through the top of the head; sometimes feet first
an audible ringing or a loud crack at the moment of impact
the opposite of a cork leaving a bottle
a hard 'thud' — one experiencer got 'the biggest headache you can imagine'
the trigger is often a single thought (concern for a child, a partner, the body)

quotes.text: And then I just slammed back into my body, and I woke up, and I was crying, and everything hurt.
the next thing I know, I'm shoved back in my body, and my body feels so heavy and so dense
And as I was getting sucked back into my body, it's like, um, the opposite of a cork getting pulled out of a bottle of wine.
slammed back into my body, like a jolt right.

places.notes: Precision is essentially perfect — this idiom has no other use. Flat to cv>=18, then drops sharply at cv>=23 (2 of 181 docs). I would not over-read that: the cv>=23 stratum is small and skews toward accounts whose evidential weight comes from out-of-body veridical detail near the body, where the return is often described as gentle re-merging rather than a snap. The corpus's own coding puts 'sudden_return' at 56.4% of sequenced accounts with a mean journey position of 0.978, so the underlying phenomenon is far more common than my strict lexical measure.

places.name: The weight of the body
places.description: The immediate aftermath of return: pain floods back, and the body is experienced as intolerably heavy, dense, small, dull and slow after weightlessness. The recurring similes are clothing and confinement — a heavy wet diving suit, wet clothes, clay, a glove, a tent, a prison. Several experiencers say the grief and guilt they had been free of returns in the same instant as the physical pain.

aliases.term: it was so heavy to be back in the body
like donning a heavy, tight diving suit
a little pup tent or prison
I felt like I was wearing my body

places.regex: (back in ?to (my|the) (physical )?body|re-?enter\w+ (my|the) body|returned to (my|the) body)[^.]{0,130}(pain|painful|heavy|heaviness|hurt|wet suit|wetsuit|suit of|prison|cage|too small|clay|agony|excruciat|sick|awful|horrible)|(hurt|painful|agony|excruciating|heavy) (to (be|come|get) back|coming back|to re-?enter)|(coming|came|getting|got) back (in ?to (my|the) body )?(was|is|felt) (so |very |really )?(painful|excruciating|awful|horrible|heavy)
sensory: gravity felt as a novel sensation, in the joints
the body as wet, heavy clothing you must put back on
slow, dull, dense — 'the physical here, it seems dead'
emotional pain returns simultaneously with physical pain
a small number report no pain at all: 'I popped back into my body, and it didn't hurt'

quotes.text: It was so heavy to be back in the body.
When she finally put me back into my body, the transition felt like donning a heavy, tight diving suit.
So I snapped back into my body and coming back to my form was excruciatingly painful.
it brought me back into my body and it was just I have to say it was just horrible because I felt from this expanded state of consciousness back into this constricted

places.notes: Doubles across the strata (1.60% -> 3.31%), monotone. Very high precision. This is the quietest and least-discussed part of the arc, but it is the emotional inverse of the peace that opens the experience, and experiencers reach for the same small set of clothing metaphors independently of one another, which is worth flagging to whoever builds the alias graph.
